name: Testolactone (Teslac)
lead: Testolactone, sold as Teslac, is a steroidal first-generation aromatase inhibitor that was used as an anticancer drug for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It was first approved in the United States in 1970 and was discontinued in 2008.[1]

Because aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, aromatase inhibitors have been of interest in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles for managing estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia. Testolactone has been described as having been studied in men for infertility, gynecomastia and growth in children, but it is no longer available for medical use and is superseded by later agents.[1][2][3]
No published trial has tested testolactone for appearance outcomes.

paras: Testolactone treated breast cancer in postmenopausal women or women whose ovaries no longer functioned, by lowering estrogen production. It was also used to delay precocious puberty and to treat gynecomastia.[1] Aromatase inhibitors, including testolactone, were examined in men with infertility and abnormal testosterone-to-estradiol ratios.[2][3]

No cosmetic indication exists. Interest in aromatase inhibitors in bodybuilding concerns controlling estrogenic effects of androgens; reviews on aromatase and gynecomastia describe estrogen's role in breast tissue growth in men.[4]

Commonly reported effects included tingling or abnormal skin sensations, limb aches, general discomfort, hair loss, loss of appetite, nausea, redness of the tongue and vomiting. Rarer serious effects included allergic reactions, edema and bone pain.[1]

Testolactone inhibits aromatase, lowering estrogen synthesis; in vitro studies suggest the inhibition may be noncompetitive and irreversible. At a high daily dose in men, estradiol fell by 25 to 50 percent after 6 to 10 days, a smaller reduction than later aromatase inhibitors produce.[1] It has very weak androgen receptor affinity and is classed as a first-generation, steroidal (Type I) inhibitor.[1]
Testolactone is a synthetic 18-oxasteroid, a D-homo analogue of androstenedione in which a six-membered lactone replaces the D ring (formula C19H24O3).[1]

Testolactone was first approved in the United States in 1970 as an antineoplastic and was discontinued in 2008.[1] Later aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole replaced it in male infertility research.[2]

Studies in men are about hormones and fertility, not appearance. A 2001 study compared testosterone-to-estradiol ratios in 63 infertile men with controls and tested an oral aromatase inhibitor; a 2002 study evaluated anastrozole in 140 subfertile men, citing earlier improvements with testolactone.[2][3] NIH-registered trials examined testolactone in precocious puberty in girls and boys and in a three-drug regimen for congenital adrenal hyperplasia in children.[5][6][7] A 2000 study reported that flutamide, testolactone and reduced hydrocortisone maintained normal growth in children with CAH.[8] No studies were found testing testolactone for muscle or other appearance goals.

timeline.event: First approved in the US for breast cancer.[1]
NIH trial in girls with precocious puberty begins.[5]

quick.overview:
Testolactone (Teslac) was a prescription aromatase inhibitor approved in the US in 1970 for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It was discontinued in 2008.

It was also studied in children with precocious puberty and in infertile men. No trial has examined it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It blocks the aromatase enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, with lowering of estradiol that is modest compared with newer drugs.
quick.risks: Reported effects include tingling, aches, hair loss, nausea and vomiting, with rarer allergic reactions and edema. It is no longer available for medical use.
